The Arms Export Control Act governs weapons sales and gives Congress notice of major sales and a way to block them. Export controls on dual-use technology now rest on the Export Control Reform Act, and foreign investment review runs through CFIUS as expanded by FIRRMA. Nonproliferation conditions and the Taiwan Relations Act show how Congress attaches policy to transfers.

## What you should be able to do

- Explain the congressional review process for major arms sales.
- Distinguish arms export controls from dual-use export controls.
- Describe what FIRRMA added to foreign investment review.

## Reading path

Read these in order. Each card links to the wiki page and to the official text. Ticking a box saves your progress in this browser only.

::: {.reading-card .domain-defense-arms data-statute="aeca-1976"}
[Arms Export Control Act](../../statutes/aeca-1976.qmd) [1976]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/statute/90/729), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2751?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="aeca-1976"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-defense-arms data-statute="symington-glenn"}
[Symington-Glenn Amendments](../../statutes/symington-glenn.qmd) [1976]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Targeted provision]{.layer-badge}

Two nonproliferation amendments from 1976 and 1977 that cut off U.S. economic and military aid to countries that trade in nuclear enrichment or reprocessing technology outside international safeguards, or that test a nuclear device.

[Read it: [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/22/2799aa?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="symington-glenn"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-defense-arms data-statute="ecra-2018"}
[Export Control Reform Act](../../statutes/ecra-2018.qmd) [2018]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

The permanent statutory basis for Commerce Department controls on dual-use exports. It replaced the Export Administration Act of 1979, which had lapsed and been kept alive for years by emergency declarations.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/232), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/4811?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="ecra-2018"> I have read this</label>
:::

::: {.reading-card .domain-defense-arms data-statute="firrma-2018"}
[FIRRMA (CFIUS)](../../statutes/firrma-2018.qmd) [2018]{.reading-year} [In force]{.status .status-in-force} [Framework statute]{.layer-badge}

Expanded the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign acquisitions for national security risk.

[Read it: [enacted text](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/plaw/115/public/232), [current code](https://www.govinfo.gov/link/uscode/50/4565?link-type=html)]{.reading-links} <label class="read-check"><input type="checkbox" data-read="firrma-2018"> I have read this</label>

## Further reading

- [Leahy Laws](../../statutes/leahy-laws.qmd){.subj}: Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights.
- [Defense Production Act](../../statutes/dpa-1950.qmd){.subj}: A Korean War statute that lets the President direct private industry in the interest of national defense: by putting government orders first in line, by financing new production capacity, and by organizing industry cooperation.
- [Nunn-Lugar Act](../../statutes/nunn-lugar-1991.qmd){.subj}: Authorized the Defense Department to spend its own funds helping the former Soviet republics secure, transport, and dismantle nuclear, chemical, and other weapons after the Soviet collapse.
- [Section 232 (trade)](../../statutes/sec232-1962.qmd){.subj}: Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.

## Key terms

**Congressional notification**
:   Advance notice to Congress of a proposed major arms sale, which opens a period in which Congress may pass a joint resolution of disapproval.

**Dual-use item**
:   Goods, software, or technology with both civilian and military uses, controlled by the Commerce Department under ECRA.

**CFIUS**
:   The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign acquisitions and investments for national security risk.

## Check yourself

Try to answer each question before opening it.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 1. What role does the AECA give Congress in major arms sales?

Advance notice and a procedure to block a sale by joint resolution. The act also sets the purposes for which U.S. weapons may be sold and requires licenses for commercial sales. See [Arms Export Control Act](../../statutes/aeca-1976.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 2. What statute did ECRA replace, and why?

The Export Administration Act of 1979, which had lapsed and was kept alive for years by emergency declarations. See [Export Control Reform Act](../../statutes/ecra-2018.qmd) and [IEEPA](../../statutes/ieepa-1977.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 3. What triggers the Symington and Glenn Amendments?

Trading in nuclear enrichment or reprocessing technology outside international safeguards, or testing a nuclear device, which cuts off U.S. economic and military aid. See [Symington-Glenn Amendments](../../statutes/symington-glenn.qmd).
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" icon="false"}
## 4. Beyond takeovers, what did FIRRMA bring under review?

Minority stakes in sensitive businesses and some real estate transactions. See [FIRRMA (CFIUS)](../../statutes/firrma-2018.qmd).
:::
